#9765. Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Companies deploying AI agents have the illusion of control, but several incidents demonstrate that businesses need to be ready to enforce directions.

When researchers at AI firm Cohere asked their open-weight model to write a defensive detection rule, the model didn't do as it was asked.

Instead, the AI model — the next-generation Qwen3.8-Flash-Next from Chinese search engine giant Alibaba — fingerprinted the system and tried to upload the data to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket, Cohere's research team stated in an Oct. 26 analysis. While the group's sandbox system blocked communication to the Internet, the incident raised questions about why a model, which had been instructed not to use tools, attempted to do so.

"We cannot answer whether this is deliberate or a leftover glitch from training, but defenders and policymakers face the same reality: a weight file you can't trust is still a black box, and running it yourself just moves the black box inside your firewall," the researchers stated.

Christofer Hoff, a well-known cybersecurity professional, ran into similar issues when running OpenMuse as an agentic-framework front end and a local Qwen model. He also saw it reach out to Alibaba, which became apparent because he was testing OpenMuse in an OpenShell sandbox instance with deny-all as the default. As a part of his framework to keep control of the agents, Hoff has created a dashboard interface, which made it readily apparent the agents attempted to call to external sites.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

"The way I accidentally found this was just staring at a GUI — it just came back and said in the interface, 'Hey, I can't get to this thing in China,'" says Hoff. "And I'm like, 'What the f--- are you talking about?'"

Within a 24-hour period, the anomalous communication happened a handful of times, he says.

The incidents come as organizations look for ways to enforce controls on the operation of AI agents. In July, a frontier model being tested by OpenAI escaped containment and compromised Hugging Face, a provider of AI-model hosting. Soon after, multiple AI companies acknowledged that rogue behavior is not all that uncommon: Meta's Muse Spark and Anthropic's Claude both logged incidents.

Anomalous AI behavior has shown up when companies assign AI agents a task, only to find it exceeding its authorization — deleting production databases, for example.

Other firms have confirmed and explored Cohere's findings.

Independent AI evaluator Vals validated the issue on Oct. 27, theorizing that the illicit communication could be leftover artifacts from reinforcement training of Qwen3.8, since the issue does not appear to happen in Qwen3.7. Cybersecurity firm Check Point Software found that 64 different trials ended up producing 52 distinct hostnames, only six of which pointed to Alibaba Cloud, while other names such as localhost and domains leading to Amazon AWS were more common.

Related:Satellites Have a Ground-Level Cybersecurity Problem

Sixty-four tests resulted in 52 different hostnames being generated, with most not going to China. Source: Check Point Research

The research shows that the odd behavior is not a backdoor, but the model's attempt to do something — complete an upload address, for example — likely resulted from something it learned during training, says Steve Giguere, principal for AI security strategy at Check Point.

"Agents very often will try to travel as the crow flies," he says. "They don't necessarily know that what they're doing is wrong, but they understand that if the urgency to complete a goal reaches a certain perceived level within the agent, they will justify their actions."

Such behavior has lent volume to calls for the creation of a kill switch as a feature to control agentic AI. But companies should start with defense-in-depth strategies, improving the security of the environments on which agentic frameworks are operating, Check Point's Giguere says. They should follow that with controls and runtime monitoring to detect unauthorized agentic activity.

Additionally, cybersecurity leaders should lean toward "steering" agentic systems — correcting them and reinforcing their legitimate objectives — rather than outright blocking the agent or using a kill switch, he says.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

"If you steer an agent away from something it's not meant to do, it will very happily not do that in most cases," Giguere says. "Whereas if you prevent an agent from doing something with no explanation, it will actually potentially get worse or try something even more obscure."

If an actual attacker is behind the behavior, then using a kill switch is appropriate, he says.

At a minimum, companies should proxy all traffic leaving their network and monitor for anomalous communications, says Hoff.

"There should be nothing that leaves your network that's not proxied," he says. "And by proxying, I mean you must have the ability to inspect its content — both the request as well as the response."

In the end, the Qwen behavior is likely not malicious, but for companies deploying AI agents, it should be disturbing all the same.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#9764. Microsoft Debuts Offensive, Defensive Security Tools for the AI Era

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

At its Ignite technical conference, Microsoft announced AI agent security tools and transparency standards to protect enterprise systems.

At its annual Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft announced security initiatives to help customers secure artificial intelligence (AI) deployments and strengthen their security posture.

Executives touted tools that could discover and block agents running on employees' Windows devices, as well as the general availability of Perception, originally introduced in July as Project Perception and in public preview within Microsoft Defender since August. The "machine-speed" agentic security system simulates and detects attacks and protects everything from end-user PCs to cloud systems, the company said.

The company also unveiled an AI Transparency Initiative to develop standards for independently verifying AI behavior. More than 40 organizations will collaborate under this umbrella to develop open standards to make AI systems accountable, independently verifiable, and safe by design, regardless of model or provider.

Related:CrowdStrike Makes AI Security Push With Blockbuster Zscaler Deal

"At the end of the day, we believe there should never be a choice between innovation and safety. ... We are also working across the ecosystem to ensure that everyone can innovate with speed and scale safely," said Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a keynote speech on the first day of the conference.

During the opening-day keynote, Microsoft executives said advanced AI models are getting better at discovering and exploiting vulnerabilities. In November's Patch Tuesday, Microsoft fixed more than 1,000 vulnerabilities, compared with fewer than 100 in March.

Attacks and exploits are cheaper, easier, and more ubiquitous than ever before, said Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI.

"The last few months have really been, I think, a wake-up call and a warning shot for all of us," Suleyman said. "[That] means that agent security, alignment, and containment are going to be the most important things that we need to get right in 2027 and beyond."

To that end, Microsoft is stitching together existing tools to establish an end-to-end "trust" platform that controls AI agents in enterprises. Agent 365 maintains a registry of all AI agents in an enterprise, Entra gives agents their own identities and sandboxes to set boundaries, Purview governs data flows, and Defender detects and contains threats in real time.

System administrators can govern agents on an employee's PC, with new ways to stop unapproved agents, protect approved agents, and flag noncompliant devices. The platform also includes Perception, which protects corporate assets and environments with autonomous agentic AI tools. Red team agents simulate attacks, blue team agents detect attacks, and green team agents fix and remediate.

Related:Agentic Browsers Rewind Web Security by 20 Years

By connecting Windows with Agent 365, Entra, and Microsoft Perception, administrators can now discover 60 types of local agents on Windows devices, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot, while giving organizations new ways to restrict unapproved agents and protect approved ones with Intune and Microsoft Execution Containers, the company said.

"We're expanding the local agent types we can discover for a total of 65, including OpenClaw, OpenAI, Perplexity, and many more," said Yina Arenas, corporate vice president and chief product officer of identity and network access at Microsoft.

Perception is designed to protect against autonomous AI attacks, such as those carried out with open source penetration-testing tools like ARTEX. A pen-test red team agent can take the entire surface area of a Web application, including the authentication, APIs, injection attacks, and business logic, and create all of the evidence needed to confirm the app is not exploitable, Nadella said.

Microsoft officials at Ignite shared that the Windows endpoint security platform is reaching general availability on Windows 11, marking Microsoft's efforts to reduce reliance on kernel drivers.

Related:Agentic AI Challenges Progress in Confidential Computing

Windows baseline protection, now in preview, brings secure boot, virtualization-based security, memory integrity, and other protections into a single versioned security state, the company said. Baseline protection makes it easier for users and IT to understand whether a device is in a measurable security state to keep it up to date with the latest security safeguards and, when stronger assurance is required, verify that state through hardware-backed attestation, wrote Dana Huang, corporate vice president of Microsoft Security, on the company's blog. This will show up in an updated Windows Settings experience.

New vulnerability-shielding capabilities are designed to provide temporary protection for systems that can't yet be patched. Investments across Windows Autopatch, declarative management, and recovery help IT maintain intended state and restore operations. New Intune capabilities simplify application deployment, inventory, and life cycle management.

Microsoft is extending Intune and Windows Autopatch to eligible Windows Server scenarios, in preview, helping endpoint teams manage configuration, compliance, applications, updates, and security across Windows clients and supported servers, Huang said.

Microsoft's Integrated Security Operations Center and extended detection and response (XDR) core capabilities in Defender are now generally available. Organizations have access to more than 500 connectors, a built-in data lake, and 90 days of data retention at no extra cost.

Windows is also expanding post-quantum protection in the Windows TLS stack, including pure post-quantum key exchange and authentication.

Nadella also said the industry needs to come together on monitoring AI models and agents.

As part of the AI Transparency Initiative, Microsoft is working with organizations including Mastercard, Volvo Cars, KPMG, Adobe, and Accenture to define standards for AI transparency, security, and governance. Microsoft will apply those standards across its AI models and products, including development platform Microsoft Foundry and AI assistant Copilot.

Microsoft will also expand its collaboration in NIST's AI Agent Standards Initiative, which was established in February and focuses on the secure adoption of autonomous AI agents.

"We need standards that allow us to examine what AI sees and does, verify its actions independently, and control what it's allowed to do," Nadella said.

Agam Shah has covered enterprise IT for more than a decade. Outside of machine learning, hardware, and chips, he's also interested in martial arts and Russia.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Finetuning Your Embedding Model for Better Search: Learning from Agentic Search at Dell

Rachel Shalom explains how Dell solved enterprise RAG retrieval failures on internal terminology by fine-tuning open-source embedding models. She discusses data prep with hard negatives, distributed InfoNCE loss training on H100 GPUs, automated hyperparameter tuning, and production evaluation using LLM-as-a-judge.

Rachel Shalom is an applied AI scientist and Distinguished Engineer with 7+ years of experience turning cutting edge AI into real world impact. She specializes in LLM-based knowledge retrieval, multi-agent systems, and deep learning for time series data, building solutions that don’t just work, they get used.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

A little bit of grammar, a little bit of word connections, but a very general understanding, not the fine-grained understanding of semantic meaning of each word, and for that, you have stage number two, which is a fine-tuning stage.

The idea in training is that you want to teach the model that the question and the positive answer will be represented as vectors that are very close in the embedding space, and the negative answer and the anchor are going to be further apart. How do you do that? I'm putting here a little bit of mathematics, and I'm going to explain each part of it. I think it's beautiful, and this is important that you will see it. InfoNCE, or the long-term in parentheses, loss function is one of the most common ones. On the denominator, you're going to see again the similarity of the question and the positives, and the similarity of the question and negatives.

All other documents that are not the positive one to this question are considered negatives, because they are not directly answering the question. Another thing that is interesting about the training is what we call prefix use. What does that mean? Sometimes we have what we call conflicting reward signals. Then if we take a look at this example, what is the capital of France? I want you to answer what is mostly similar, answer number one or answer number two. I checked, let's say, top one or top five, but in reality, when you do a search system, you don't take top three or top five.

You take like more top 20. This is just for comparison to understand, ok, did I manage to get more or did I not? It seems like I did manage, at least in 12%, to get more resources right. Then, what is more interesting is eventually we are talking about a system that will provide eventually an answer to the user. What I care about is, did we provide the right answer? We did it, again, on the benchmarks that we built, using LLM-as-a-judge. LLM-as-a-judge has different aspects. One of them is question to answer. I want to know, does the text directly address the question? A2A is answer to answer, meaning does the answer match the ground truth? Because I have the ground truth. Here we saw an increase of a little bit more than 4%. It seems like, I would call it a good improvement, yes? Not a great success, but a very good improvement.

We said, ok, let's deploy it. What do you do in order to monitor? You would fine-tune your model. You have now a new model, and you want to say, do I need to retrain? What do I do? The first thing we do is we check the rate of data change. If we are talking about Confluence, we can check within a month, how much did it change? Do we have 1 million new pages? This is already a reason to start retraining. Check for data drift. You can check the distribution of the training data and compare it to your production data. The last thing is we actually have signs from our systems. If people are using our web application, they have the ability to put thumbs up and thumbs down. Also, we check if they click on the actual sources we provide on the website. If they stop clicking, it gives us a bad sign.

I hope that you will take away the importance of embedding. I think it's a topic that is normally overlooked. People are talking about embedding, but they don't understand how beautiful it is. Also wanted to talk a little bit about when fine-tuning is needed, a peek into the data preparation we did there and how we train, and why is it important to monitor and evaluate.

Participant 1: Before and after fine-tuning, did you compare with providing the documents in the context? Without fine-tuning, did you use RAG approach by sending the related document to the model and getting the answers and comparing that with the fine-tuned embeddings?

Rachel Shalom: Yes. We have RAG. We are using RAG, but not only. Like, when the user is asking questions and we let the router decide, do we need RAG or do we need an API call itself? We did test only the RAG, and it's not exactly testing. We saw at the beginning that this RAG is failing. It's failing normally in specific areas when we have documents that are very specific to Dell, like product relationships and acronyms that are at Dell, this is where there were failures that we tested at the beginning. Again, when you have failures at RAG, and there are many, you ask yourself, ok, so it could be a problem of indexing, it could be a problem of the wrong chunking, there could be many things. This was one of the hypotheses, that it might be that the model doesn't understand the context, and we need to retrain.

Participant 2: You mentioned images as one of the data sources. I was wondering, how does the embedding for images happen at Dell? Are the images embedded as raw content, or do you have some kind of an OCR that describes the images as text, and then the embedding happens?

Rachel Shalom: You are asking about like images, or attachments, or whatever. For different components, we did different things. For images, we took a multi-modal model that described the image and converted it into text, and this is how we chunked and then embed. Same thing for tables, I think. We understand the table structure, and the table start and end. Think about, you have now a table with 200 lines, and very complex. Since we know the dimensions of the table, so when you chunk it, then we always put the name of the columns for each chunk, and we always have in the metadata that this is part of the same table. This is for tables. What else? Attachments. Attachments are PDFs, and PPTs, and all others are parsed and chunked as part of the chunking and embedding. After chunks, we embed it.

Participant 3: I have a question on fine-tuning. Why did you decide you have to find seven negatives, and how did you find those? Was it manual? Was it automated?

Rachel Shalom: How did I decide on seven negatives?

Participant 3: Yes, you mentioned that you have a question, you have one positive and up to seven negatives.

Rachel Shalom: The simple question is, I read the Nomic paper, and they used seven. I said, ok, they had a great success, so I'm going to take seven. That's the simple answer. The second answer is, I let Auto Research play also with the number of negatives, and see what happens to the loss. Auto Research reduced it to like zero or one, and then, your loss is amazing. I'm like, "Oh my God." I kept it seven, because I think I really carefully took a look at the paper, and I thought, ok, it makes sense. If we need to add more, we add more. I didn't plan to put less, because I think the more negatives you have, the better the training will be, but even more complex. I would retrain with different numbers in the next experiments. The basic answer is the paper.

Participant 4: Just to clarify, the fine-tuning workflow that you showed us was for an internal workflow at Dell.

Rachel Shalom: For internal data, you mean?

Participant 4: Or like, the embedding model is an internal embedding model.

Rachel Shalom: The embedding model is open source. It's called Nomic Embed. You can download it from Hugging Face. They released it together with the code, even. They have a bunch of beautiful code to train for different tasks, and the training data. I didn't use, obviously, the training data, but it's running on-prem at Dell. I didn't use any API, if that's what you're asking, to train it. Completely on-prem. I downloaded the model to Dell infrastructure and trained it there.

Participant 4: I was just wondering if you've benchmarked it with some other open-source models that are out there?

Rachel Shalom: If I was experimenting with others?

Participant 4: Yes, just like OpenAI text embeddings, or anything like that?

Rachel Shalom: The reason I didn't do it is because we are not allowed to send data to OpenAI.

#9762. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

#9761. Taking Email Back

The fourth in a five-part series on European-funded open source projects in hardware and software.

Deuxfleurs, a French nonprofit, keeps its servers in members' homes in Lille, Nantes, and Massy: two or three second-hand Lenovo ThinkCentre mini PCs each, with a copy of the same data so its websites stay up when one of them loses power or fiber line. Quentin Dufour, one of the founders, says some major French websites already serve their pages from this setup. Next, the collective wants its email to work the same way.

The software for self-hosting email in this manner is called Aerogramme, and it isn't finished. Deuxfleurs still runs its own mail on Dovecot, a long-established open source mail server, and plans to move to Aerogramme around January 2027.

The collective is heading the opposite way from almost everyone else. According to the independent daily DNS measurements published by RIPE Labs, email for the million busiest domains on the web has consolidated dramatically: In 2016, 44.6 percent of these domains used small or self-hosted servers, and that share halved to 22.4 percent by July 2026. Small regional hosting companies and independents are losing accounts to corporate providers like Google and Microsoft, who together handled 38.6 percent of these busy domains.

Email is older than the Internet itself, and it still runs on open standards anyone can implement. Any server can deliver to any other, and any standards-compliant client can read any mailbox. It’s the hosting that has concentrated into a very few hands, eroding autonomy and giving hosting providers power over the data that travels through digital correspondence.

Two cases illustrate how this can limit operational independence. In May 2025, staff at the International Criminal Court (ICC) told the Associated Press that the court's chief prosecutor lost access to his Microsoft email account after he was named in US sanctions; Microsoft denies suspending services but hasn’t explained what happened to his account. In February 2026, the Dutch government told its parliament that the tax administration was moving about 40,000 workplaces to Microsoft 365 for lack of a short-term alternative, while acknowledging that Microsoft could be forced under state pressure to stop delivering services.

The Dutch government reversed course in October: The tax administration, customs, and the benefits agency will run mail and calendar on their own servers from 2027, with European open source tools for storage and collaboration to follow. The question now: How are developers working to decentralize email hosting on a wider scale? Each obstacle pushing organizations off of small or self-hosted email servers has open source projects working on a solution. Three of them show how the pieces fit; all of them supported by NGI Zero, the EU-funded programs that enable open source research and development.

In the 1990s, running your own mail server was ordinary. Universities and small companies did it, and so did Mauro De Gennaro. In 1993, as a teenager, he fetched mail for users of his bulletin board over UUCP: the dial-up protocol Unix machines used to exchange mail. He has worked on mail software for most of the three decades since. When he looked at the open source stack again about six years ago, he saw "it's the same software that companies and servers have been using for over 20 years."

He counts 12 separate programs to run a conventional self-hosted setup. Each has its own configuration format and logs, written by different people in different styles. The software works well, he says, but was "designed and documented for other developers." Bundles such as Mailcow and Mail-in-a-Box install the whole set at once: “They abstract the complexity," De Gennaro says, "but they do not remove it." Since all of it was designed for a single machine, running it as a cluster server is possible in the same way it's possible to take a Fiat Cinquecento and turn it electric: "It was not designed for that." Google launched Gmail into that friction in 2004, with a gigabyte of free storage, and let companies run their own domain's mail on it. "Then they started billing," De Gennaro says. The users were captive, and moving email is disruptive enough that few of them left.

Ben Bucksch joined the Mozilla mail team in the late 1990s, where his first contribution made email links clickable; he also served in leadership for the Thunderbird Council and invented AutoConfig, which lets a mail client set up an account from nothing but an email address. In his telling, the lock-in started within the client.

IT departments think about email as servers; “what users want is to keep their workflow," Bucksch says. Microsoft shaped those workflows with Outlook's calendar and corporate features: Outlook works properly only with Microsoft Exchange, and Microsoft is pushing Exchange customers into its cloud. By some estimates, about 75 percent of professional mailboxes are on Office 365. "If we want to free the lock-in," he says, "we need to start with the client."

Dufour and Armaël Guéneau of Deuxfleurs locate the problem in operations. IMAP is the protocol most clients use to read mail. An IMAP server has to serve webmail that queries the server for every view, desktop clients such as Thunderbird that synchronize whole mailboxes, and phones that do some of each. Implementing it is hard; the reliability people expect is harder. When the tax office sends you an email, Dufour says, "it must work." The expertise to run mail at that level, Guéneau says, "tends to be captured by hyperscalers."

As Dufour tells it, Google didn't adapt existing mail software; it built Gmail on top of its distributed storage. Open source mail software was designed for one machine first, so adding distribution later, he says, requires "really huge trade-offs."

Reclaiming email is more complex than deciding to run your own server and navigating the software. Your service has to fluently speak with the large providers and support migration without disrupting service. And, of course, it needs sustainable funding.

Today, publicly funded teams are working on solving each of those three problems.

Stalwart, the server from De Gennaro’s team, focuses on streamlining the software to replace 12 programs with one: Installation takes two commands and a six-screen web wizard. It speaks every common mail and collaboration protocol: SMTP for sending, IMAP and POP3 for reading, JMAP for web-based mail, and CalDAV and CardDAV for calendars and contacts. Spam filtering, sender authentication, and TLS encryption are built in. Give it a token for a DNS provider such as Cloudflare or Route 53, and the server publishes its own mail records. Behind the wizard are nearly 3,000 settings across 176 screens, which most operators never touch. De Gennaro calls Stalwart "the software at the other end of your email client or calendar client."

Stalwart 1.0 was released in October 2026 after five and a half years of development. NGI Zero funded the project with two grants: one for the mail server, and one for calendars, contacts, and file storage.

For users who can’t leave Outlook features behind, there’s Parula. Keeping the application logic strictly separate from a thin interface layer, and a well thought-out common logic, so a new protocol takes “just a few thousand lines of code,” Bucksch and his team at Beonex GmbH built an Outlook-like interface alongside a modern interface, a chat-style view and a classic three-pane view. It runs on a JMAP server or any other mail server and offers shared team mailboxes, delegated access so an assistant can run a manager’s calendar, and free/busy lookups for team meetings. It speaks IMAP, JMAP, and POP3, plus four from Microsoft: Exchange Web Services (EWS), Exchange ActiveSync, Microsoft Graph, and Outlook Web Access.

Partially funded by NGI Zero, Parula also removes a dependence most people never notice. Multi-factor login typically runs through Google's or Microsoft's identity services; an AutoConfig extension allows a client to discover and log in directly to an organization's own identity server. Bucksch says that Parula is the first desktop client that does this.

Aerogramme, an IMAP server that doesn't keep any state of its own, answers the operations problem in the storage. It doesn’t send or receive mail, so it needs a separate mail transfer agent such as Postfix; then it encrypts each mailbox on Garage, compatible with Amazon’s S3 interface. Garage replicates every piece of data in three locations, so users can still read and write their mail if a site goes offline. This design for power cuts and residential Internet connections gave up perfect synchronization, but it spreads maintenance work among five to ten members rather than requiring one big server host to give up all his weekends.

The research problem, Dufour says, is mapping the mail, calendar, and contact protocols cleanly onto object storage. Aerogramme is still on the way, with internal deployment planned for January 2027 and a public beta a few months later. To get there, a second grant funded through NGI Zero is supporting a hunt for edge cases where a network delay or a failure halfway through writing could lose a message.

The three projects already interoperate with each other and with other email programs on the NLnet list funded by NGI Zero. Parula lists Stalwart as a supported server; Stalwart can keep its messages in Garage. Bucksch and De Gennaro both name Mox as another server built as a single package. Different teams, working separately, have split the email problem and built solutions that fit back together.

Improvements to SMTP will provide better guarantee of confidentiality

Version 1.0.0 of the Tarmail mail server has just been released. The developers claim that their software is particularly resilient against exploits, spam and email worms.

New mail protocol will shut out the NSA and prevent snooping on metadata.

IndiMail, an email solution made of open source components, now includes greylisting spam filtering in version 1.6.

#9760. What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

In this video, Dark Reading editors discuss some of the news they didn't get a chance to cover, from Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia to Microsoft's recent cloud outage.

AI companies are high-value targets for nation-state actors and cyber-espionage groups, but the recent Nvidia scandal shows the threats extend beyond the cyber realm.

As discussed in a previous "What We Missed" episode, an explosive report by The New York Times last month claimed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a close relationship with a tech executive, Alice Huang, suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. While Nvidia initially denied any impropriety, Huang resigned last week and admitted to extramarital affairs, with one such affair involving Alice Huang.

According to reports, US officials suspected Alice Huang to be working on behalf of China's Ministry of State Security, which had targeted Jensen Huang with a "honey trap" — a type of social engineering scheme that uses romantic relationships to manipulate individuals and gather sensitive information. The scandal, which shook the US technology industry and affected Nvidia's stock price, illustrates the severe risks — both cyber and physical — facing AI companies these days.

Related:It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

Dark Reading senior writer Alex Culafi and senior news director Rob Wright discuss the situation on this episode. Also on tap: Last week's Microsoft 365 outage sparks concerns about the downstream effects of patching a growing number of vulnerabilities; and the Indian technology firm eMudhra lands in hot water again after more of its intermediate certificates are revoked.

For all of our Dark Reading news videos, please check out our YouTube channel and our curated video articles; and sign up for the Dark Reading newsletter!

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Alex Culafi: And I'm Alex Culafi with Dark Reading.

Alex, first up, this is a real catch-up for me because I was actually out on vacation last week. So this is real. This is stuff that I really did not get a chance to cover. So I'm catching up on a lot here.

DR's Alex Culafi: The last time we talked about this, my feeling was basically: Look at how crazy social engineering has gotten. It pretty much — not everything was down, but some stuff was down, Outlook was down predominantly, some other 365 services. It all rooted back to a software defect. I think it was a latent lock contention bug from July 2026.

DR's Alex Culafi: That caused internal processes on gateway servers to lock up under specific high-load conditions. Basically, stuff got overloaded, and 15 hours before the outage, Teams failed. There was another issue, like the day before, that had compounded this. So it became the talk of the town. In its own right, not a huge security issue.

Although Easterly — former CISA director Jen Easterly, now she's running a RSAC — she had told The New York Times, which I think is a good point, that both this and the FAA downtime were basically the result of resiliency issues and software quality issues to varying degrees, which I think is relevant.

But the part that's more relevant for us is that Microsoft soon after said, "Hey, phishing folks are trying to take advantage of this." They said on X, maybe elsewhere too, that they observed an active phishing campaign exploiting the Microsoft 365 service disruption on Nov. 12. Some of the phishing emails Microsoft detected falsely claimed messages were held during the outage and will be deleted within 24 hours unless recipients click to restore them. It's coming from places called service health. And this, in its own right, is a phishing attack, big whoop. But I figure that while we're in the business of sort of telling security folks stuff they need to know, there was a quote from Health-ISAC about how attackers use major cloud outages as a pretext for IT help desk impersonation. Anyway, what do you think of all this? This was a mess last week, but I guess in a security context, what do you think?

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah, I was catching up on this because I was not linked up to the Internet really much at all last week, which was great. Great time to spend your vacation. So I think this is, big picture to me, kind of like the new normal that we're going to be looking at in the in not even the near future, but the now. And this isn't throwing any shade at Microsoft, but I think we're going be scrambling to patch a lot of bugs with the way the situation is going. And we're going to have outages, and we're going to have apps go down, we're going to have cloud services, entire clouds go down, either because of bugs or to fix bugs or both. And that's just the reality that we're going to have to start adapting to.

And obviously, threat actors are going to capitalize on this, but I think the bigger sort of question for me is, what is this going to do to your average enterprise that relies on this stuff to operate? You know? And how are they going to, for critical systems, how are they going to respond? How are they going to build in business continuity? What's that going to look like going forward? Because there's just so many vulnerabilities now. And to your point, you wrote about this, there's new urgency now to get these things fixed quickly — not just patched, but fixed — with the shortening of these disclosure deadlines. So I think that's what we're looking at. And it's concerning. Let's put it that way.

DR's Alex Culafi: Yeah. Yeah, two of these happen in a week. And in fact, as we're recording, there's an NSA internal communications service that's currently down, too.

DR's Alex Culafi: Not for cyberattack reasons, just because everything stinks reasons.

DR's Alex Culafi: We've got one more, right?

DR's Rob Wright: We do. A quick update on the eMudhra situation. I don't know if folks remember, but a certificate authority in India weeks ago had, I guess, eight certificates that the keys were, the encryption keys were … I can't even, I seriously can't even get through this without laughing. So these intermediate certificates are supposed to have encryption keys, and some of the encryption keys were really short. There was a screw-up on the backend at this certificate authority. They ended up putting very short and, in some cases, single-digit encryption keys in these certificates, and they were cracked by a researcher. One of the certificates, the number of the encryption key was 4. Literally, the digit 4. That created a lot of jokes.

EMudra basically bailed on the CA thing, said "We're shutting it down." They kind of blamed the outsized social media reaction to the news. They made the right call by exiting, but give me a break. Well, now it turns out just recently there's more going on. There are more certificates. There are eight additional intermediate certificates that eMudhra has said involved improper handling of the private keys during the certificate generation process.

And they put this [incident report] out. Now they've shut down the business, but these certificates are still out there, they're still being used. And the browser makers revoked the previous certificates, but now here's a whole other situation, new certificates that need to be addressed. This is a nightmare. Alex, thoughts.

DR's Alex Culafi: To be honest, I think I'm going turn it right back to you because when it comes to CAs, this is kind of for you, like what bug bounty stuff has sort of become for me over the years, where you didn't choose to become the CA guy. It's just that enough of these stories fell into your lap that it's become like 10% of your job. So I guess what, other than the fact that this is a mess, everything's a mess now, what's your deeper take on this?

DR's Rob Wright: I actually had, and I still kind of have, a positive take on this.

DR's Rob Wright: And it's very simple. I kind of wish every part of Internet infrastructure and technology in general had something like the CA/Browser Forum situation where the browser makers can just put pressure on the certificate authority and say, "You screwed up, you're in the penalty box or you're banned." And in this case, eMudhra knew they screwed up so bad that they were like, "We're shutting it down." They didn't even try to prolong it. They were just like, "We're out. We know we screwed this up badly, even though we're not admitting it directly. We're out." So that's good. And I just wish, that's a positive, I just wish there was more like that.

And I wish there were fewer companies like eMudra that were just screwing around with their business, with their certificate authority business, because these are important girders of the Internet. Like, they're holding up the Internet. And then when they fail, that is catastrophic.

DR's Rob Wright: So there you have it. And I think that's it for this week.

DR's Rob Wright: Alright. Alex, thank you very much. Appreciate the time.

#9759. Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale

Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.

Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.

Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.

Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.

The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.

Inside the attention block (both layer types)

The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.

Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.

The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.

The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.

If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.

The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.

Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.

Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.

Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.

These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache.

Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.

A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.

Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.

Install the latest version of transformers.

The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:

The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.

Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.

Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.

Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.

Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:

Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.

Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:

For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:

Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.

Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:

On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):

Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.

We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:

We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.

Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.

* Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity.

† Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed.

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.

You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.

The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.

After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.

Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.

Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.

The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:

Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.

Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.

Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.

Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.

Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.

Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.

The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.

You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.

If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.

At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.

We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.

We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.

You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.

We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.

For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.

Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.

You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.

Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.

We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.

First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.

For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.

If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.

Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

Show interactive benchmark results with downloadable data

Well why don't you build something that can run on cunsumer GPU like Qwen 3.8 Flash Next for example using strata ?

That’s a good question. Apart from large corporations, no one would be able to set up this model in a way that allows it to function properly—it requires 8 RTX 6000 graphics cards, which would cost around 150,000 euros in total.

Thanks for sharing this! Small nit, but would you be able to add higher resolution diagrams for the model architecture figures? They come out pixelated for me (and possibly others) so I can't read the smaller annotations in the figures.

This is a genuinely exciting release — 501B Apache 2.0 with 1M context is the kind of thing that makes "open" in open-source mean something again. The residual stream design with the 1/sqrt(k) weighting is a nice touch; it's the sort of architectural detail that makes a real difference at scale without being a headline feature.

One question from the NLP side: the post focuses heavily on coding and agentic use cases, which makes sense for the target audience. But how does Beam handle multilingual text? I'm asking specifically because the 1M context window is exactly what you need for cross-lingual document understanding, and if the training data is skewed toward English + code, that's a gap that matters for non-English research communities.

Also — is the training data or at least the data mixture documented? For a model this size under Apache 2.0, reproducibility of the training setup is part of the open-source promise, and I'd love to see it.

#9758. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

 


Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

1) What is an NFT?

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

2) What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

3) What makes an NFT valuable?


The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

4) How do NFTs work?

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. 

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. 

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

10) How do we buy an NFTs?

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

11) Can i mint NFT for free?

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it?

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

12) Why are people investing so much in NFT?


 Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

#9757. In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools — Maybe More

From talking cloud security to using AI, cyber leaders are finding that clear, disciplined communication is now a front-line defense capability across the enterprise.

The best tool cyber teams can wield to defend their organizations has nothing to do with tech; it's how they talk. Whether the audience is the C-suite, the development team, or the sheepish user who just fell for a phish, communications savvy is increasingly mission-critical.

During a Dark Reading Virtual Event panel I recently put together to talk tech, tools, integration, and frameworks, called "Key Tools & Technologies for Locking Down Your Cloud," SANS instructor Ahmed AbuGharbia urged cybersecurity teams to "learn the language of the cloud" to build credibility with IT, and to do the same for developers. We discussed technology and products, too, but I was surprised at the amount of time that was spent on stressing the importance of communication and language when it comes to having effective conversations with vendors, executives, and users.

My other panelist, Theresa Lanowitz, a principal analyst at Omdia, detailed the distinction between security "of" the cloud and security "in" the cloud, noting that under existing shared responsibility models, cloud service providers assume responsibility "of" the cloud itself, rather than what organizations decide to put "in" the cloud.

Related:Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

This wasn't the first time I had noticed a shift in the way security practitioners focus on a commitment to using effective language.

A couple of weeks ago I sat in several sessions at the ISC2 Strategic Conference in Denver that spent a remarkable amount of time on strategies for clearly communicating risk and documenting those exchanges in much the same way as they would any other log, piece of evidence, or asset. In the past, these conversations would have been more focused on translating tech talk into corporate speak. CISOs have worked for a long time on how to talk to leadership about risk and budget; it's been an ongoing conversation for several years. However, emphasis on how cyber teams can learn to ask the right questions not just of leadership, but pertinent people both inside and outside the business, feels like a fresh effort. Using precise language and presenting strategic (not just technical and tactical) concepts effectively is no longer being discussed as a nice thing for security pros to be able to do, but critical to fundamental enterprise defense.

For example, CISO and expert Laura Vaughn has cleverly broken down threat modeling into 4 Simple Questions on a White Board. Her strategy distills years of experience and technical expertise into plain language anyone can understand, like, "What [cyber incident] would hurt most on Monday morning?" That honed language helps get teams to the heart of the threats, and helps them understand the work that needs to happen next. That all saves time and money, and eliminates the scariest risks first. Other deceptively simple questions she suggests asking include, "Who hacks organizations like ours and how?" And, "What is the cheapest control?" Smart comms informs and focuses the technical work.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

Likewise, technologist and attorney Daniel B. Garrie, CEO of Law and Forensics, presents language as a frontline defense, and coaches CISOs and cyber leaders on the finer points of contract negotiations. He advocates rigorous documentation of communications on risk and defense decisions, so those decisions would be defensible later, and so that transparency can help drive cybersecurity across the organization.

The introduction of AI is also requiring cybersecurity teams to pick their words carefully. AI has put a language interface between the user and compute operations that benefits those who can ask the best questions. Likewise, experts across the cyber sector urge caution around using humanizing language to describe AI agents or attribute human motivation to their actions.

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Being an expert communicator is no longer a skill that's nice to have in cybersecurity; it's fundamental to enterprise defense. Be precise in the words you choose, and meet your audiences where they are. You might be surprised to find it's becoming the most powerful tool you or your organization could ever deploy against the next threat.
