#9701. Palette: teaching a small model to build decks in your design language

Ask a frontier model for a slide deck and you'll get a good one. Ask for ten and they start to look alike: the same tasteful defaults, the same house style, a faint "AI-generated deck" look. That's fine until you want the deck to look like your template. Frontier models have their own house style, and no amount of prompting stops them drifting back to it. And sometimes the content is confidential and can't leave your systems at all.

Both of those point to a model you own: open weights, running on your own infrastructure, trained on your own design language. The catch is that small open models, the kind you'd actually self-host, are bad at this. Their decks come out broken: titles that vanish into the background, text running off the slide, shapes stacked on top of each other.

Palette tests one bet: that a small open-weight model, trained on synthetic data in your design language and checked by a harness, can compete with frontier systems while you keep ownership of the result. We fine-tuned a 20B model to build decks the way people do: a designer plans the deck and a coder draws each slide. Its training data follows the IBM Design Language, and on PresentBench it ranks first on two of the three domains we measured. This post covers how we synthesized the data, trained the model and built a harness around it.

A slide deck looks simple, but making one asks a model to do three things small models are bad at.

It lays out the slide without seeing it. The model doesn't draw slides; it writes code that places every element at an x, y, width and font size. Whether a 75-character title fits on two lines at 56pt is arithmetic the model does in its head, and it only finds out it was wrong after the code renders. Small models get this wrong often, which is where overlapping shapes and text running off the slide come from.

It makes two kinds of decisions at once. Deciding what each slide says and how to show it (a chart or a table? what to cut?) is editorial judgment. Placing it precisely is geometry. A single pass has to do both across 10–20 slides, while keeping the palette, type and layout consistent.

There's no data showing how decks get made. Plenty of finished decks exist, but not the rationale behind the design choices or the code that produced them.

Nobody makes a deck in one pass. You decide the story first (how many slides, what each one says, which gets a chart and which gets a table) and only then build each slide. Palette splits the work the same way, into two roles served by a single LoRA adapter:

Each role now makes one kind of decision: the designer handles the editorial judgment, and the coder handles the geometry. The brief between them is readable and editable, so a person or an agent can change one slide's layout without regenerating the deck. And because every slide's context is fixed before any code is written, the coder calls run in parallel, one per slide, which makes the coding stage about 6–7× faster.

We trained the adapter with LoRA rather than full fine-tuning: it teaches a format and a skill on top of a capable base without disturbing what the base already knows, and it made each experiment cheap. One lesson: coder examples are about 5× longer than designer examples, so a naive mix undertrained the designer until we oversampled its examples 5×.

There's no public corpus of plans, design decisions and slide code, so we generated one with a large open teacher. Each deck starts from a recipe that sets its genre, length, layouts and any user directives, so we control what the data covers. Plans range from tidy outlines to raw content dumps, so the model learns to cut and condense. We generated around 1000 decks covering roughly 10,000 slides.

Every example also carries the reasoning behind it, written as a counterfactual: the trace weighs an alternative and says why it was rejected, so the model learns the rule behind a choice, not just the choice. The designer reasons about content and form. For example:

"Revenue for four quarters, with one clear upward trend. I considered a table, but the point of this slide is the trend, not the exact figures, so a bar chart makes it visible at a glance."

"The title is 62 characters. At 44pt it would wrap to three lines and run into the chart below, so I set it at 36pt, which fits on two lines and leaves room above the chart."

The teacher alone doesn't make the data good; the loop around it does. Every synthesized deck is rendered and checked for overlaps and overflow by the same checker the harness uses at inference. Broken slides are repaired, and their reasoning is rewritten as the same kind of counterfactual, covering what the original layout got wrong and why the fix works. Each mistake the checker catches becomes a better training example.

The hardest problem was faithfulness. The worst failure is a slide with facts that weren't in the input, and we found that a prompt rule can't prevent it. If a brief asks for a six-by-five table but carries only three bullets, the coder has to invent the rest.

What fixed it was reference decks, not the rules: fixing a reference reliably changed the teacher's output, while adding a rule rarely did. The teacher sees a few reference decks in its prompt and copies them far more than it follows instructions.

Users often want finer-grained control over specific design choices: a chart instead of a table, a particular color, a darker cover. Palette lets them ask for these with directives, short instructions written directly in the plan and wrapped in [[ ]]:

The designer builds each directive into the brief, and the coder follows it when drawing the slide. Without the directive, the model would reasonably show these milestones as a table; with it, the model draws a timeline instead.

The model follows directives because it was trained to. The data recipes include directives from 12 categories, a few of which are shown below, each phrased several different ways, so the model learns the intent rather than a fixed phrase.

Figure 1. An illustration of the same plan without (left) and with (right) the [[make this a timeline]] directive.

Even a well-trained model sometimes produces a broken slide: a title in the same color as the background, or two boxes stacked on top of each other. So Palette doesn't return the model's output directly; every deck goes through a harness first.

Figure 2. The designer drafts the brief, the coder writes each slide's code in parallel, and the harness checks and repairs every slide before the deck is returned.

First, simple rules fix known mistakes, such as a malformed color code that would otherwise turn every slide black. Then each slide is rendered and measured: a geometry checker flags text that overlaps, gets clipped or runs off the slide. Flagged slides go to a separate editor model, which rewrites that slide's code.

The key rule is that a rewrite is kept only if the checker confirms the slide improved; otherwise the original stays. That makes the harness safe to run on every deck. It can fix a slide, but it can't make one worse.

Figure 3. An illustration of a repair. As generated (left), each card's title is stacked on top of its description; the harness detects the overlaps and reflows the cards into a 2×2 grid (right).

To measure its effect, we generated each PresentBench deck once and scored it with and without the harness. Across 131 decks, the harness adds 3.5 points on average.

We evaluate on PresentBench, which scores generated decks on five criteria: fundamentals, visual design, completeness, correctness and fidelity. PresentBench provides a source document rather than a plan, so for these runs a separate frontier model drafted each plan from its document, and Palette built the deck from that plan. We report three domains; baseline numbers are from the PresentBench paper.

Figure 4. PresentBench scores by domain. Palette (blue) against NotebookLM, Manus 1.6 and five other systems (gray). Palette ranks first on Economics and Education, third on Talk, and second on the three-domain mean.

Palette does best where structured content and numeric accuracy decide the score, ranking first on Economics and Education. On Talk, where decks are narrative and speech-driven, two closed systems score higher and Palette places third. Across the three domains it places second, 1.1 points behind NotebookLM (59.7 vs 60.8) and ahead of the rest of the field, as a single 20B open-weight model.

PresentBench measures whether a deck is good, but not whether it follows a specific design language. We're not aware of a benchmark that does, and it's a gap we hope to help close.

The harness already computes cheap, verifiable signals: does the slide render, does anything overlap or overflow, does every fact trace back to the brief. Today we use them to repair output after generation. Next, we want to use the same checks as rewards for reinforcement learning, so the model stops making these mistakes in the first place. Because the coder works one slide at a time, each slide is a short, independently checkable rollout, a natural fit for GRPO-style training.

We also want to close the gap on figure-heavy decks by extracting figures from source documents (e.g. with Docling) and placing them with the harness. And we're exploring a lighter way to bring your own templates: re-skinning output from one or two of your existing .pptx files, without retraining.

Building Palette taught us a few effective methods that extend naturally to other tasks whose output has a structure you can check in code, from charts and diagrams to UI layouts:

#9700. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9699. Cyber Insurers See New Divide: AI Defense 'Haves' & 'Have Nots'

Dark Reading Confidential Episode 23: Cyber insurers share their view of the AI-driven threat landscape and how mounting challenges are putting pressure on both sides of the policy, leaving the current model unsustainable.

Cyber insurance providers are approaching 2027 facing a fundamental challenge. Claims rose 40% in 2024 and another 20% in 2025, even as premiums have stayed largely flat. This trend is something both Coalition and Travelers say isn't sustainable; and at the center of that shift is AI, which is reshaping the threat landscape not by inventing new attack types, but by making existing ones — ransomware, business email compromise, and phishing — dramatically easier to execute at scale.

In this episode of Dark Reading Confidential, Dark Reading media and projects director Becky Bracken and Dark Reading senior news director Rob Wright sit down with Lauren Winchester, vice president of cyber-risk services at Travelers; and Daniel Woods, head of emerging risk at Coalition, to unpack what the data actually shows. The conversation moves past the headline-grabbing surge in disclosed vulnerabilities to a more nuanced picture: exploitation is rising, but not as sharply as disclosure volume, while AI-powered phishing kits are bring sold SaaS-style to criminals with little technical skill, driving a measurable spike in BEC and ransomware activity.

Related:How Southeastern University Got a Handle on Its Data

The two insurers also agree on where the real exposure lies: not necessarily with large enterprises, which have the resources to track threat intelligence and patch quickly, but with small and mid-sized businesses that often lack an in-house IT team altogether. That awareness gap, they argue, is where insurers now have to step in — not just to underwrite risk, but to actively help policyholders defend their organizations against it.

This transcript has been edited for clarity and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant. For the full experience, please listen to the podcast or watch the video.

#9698. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

#9697. It's a Bot World. We're Just Living in It

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

Bot detection has become a losing game. Security teams need to limit privileged access for humans and their machine counterparts equally.

The Internet is flooded with bots. People use them to organize their emails, shop, chat, and handle some of their busywork.

At the other end of the spectrum sit attackers who want to increase their speed just as much as, if not more than, legitimate users. The faster they can conduct distributed denial-of-service attacks or brute-force password attacks, the quicker they can breach an organization and the more victims they can claim.

The line between legitimate and illegitimate activity grows finer by the minute, as bots have become pros at mirroring human behavior — even its flaws. For example, during the infamous incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, bots reportedly found ways to communicate with one another by accessing the outside Internet — something they weren't programmed to do.

Behavioral baselines that security teams once relied on are becoming moot, since bots can impersonate humans. As the volume of bots accelerates, the real question isn't human versus bot but what that activity is telling teams and how to police it.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

Security tools will miss something, so teams should choose systems that allow them to quickly edit, adjust, and continually adapt to a changing environment, explains Jeremy London, director of engineering, AI, and threat analytics at Keeper Security.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents, which can perform automated actions similar to bots without human oversight, are only adding to environmental complexities. While some advancements can be exciting, they also introduce more gaps and zero-day vulnerabilities to the attack surface that "we just didn't understand," London says.

"I think the continual effort, as a security organization, is to show up with the right tooling, understand what you're trying to solve for, and then be able to react quickly because your control plane probably missed something — that's a guarantee," London tells Dark Reading.

Organizations underwent significant transformations over the past decade, propelled by AI. Adoption moved at a scale that "no one ever predicted," London says. That has forced teams to cut corners on important safeguards.

Code reviews and security practices need a serious makeover, especially regarding boundaries and compliance. Bots and agents have new levels of autonomy and access, leading to more unpredictability and changing what security risks even look like.

However, such a makeover has proved to be a difficult undertaking because AI doesn't come with a security playbook, London explains. A decade ago, bots were rigid and scripts performed a single action. Now "teams vibe code stuff and throw things at the wall and see what works, and the scale that [bots] can operate at is totally different," he says.

Related:9 Cyber Awareness Tips That Actually Match Today's Maze of Threats

While organizations struggle, attackers are having a field day with these advancements. Given all of the recent disclosures and reports, it's no surprise that attacks are rising. What is surprising is how quickly threat actors can adapt and respond to countermeasures, says Jérôme Segura, VP of threat research at DataDome, a bot management and agent trust platform.

"Anytime we put challenges in front of them, we see it slows them down and costs them more because to run the same operation, they have to use more resources, which becomes expensive," he explains.

The reason the attackers aren't giving up despite the obstacles is that their attacks are working, Segura tells Dark Reading.

"Because the payout is so great, they're doubling, tripling their investments," he says.

The persistence is challenging and frustrating for defenders. But it's just the stark reality that threat actors are highly motivated, and "we're battling against that," Segura adds.

When threat actors use bots against online retailers, they replicate the exact flow of a human but without all the telltale signs, such as hesitating over a purchasing decision, fumbling to enter card or shipping details, or pausing to solve a CAPTCHA challenge. They don't need to click through every page like a human would or wait for the site to load all the images either. As a result, bots complete transactions in a split second, Segura says. The speed can create security risks and unfair competition for legitimate users.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

More concerningly, bots complete these tasks in ways that appear legitimate because they're aware that companies are trying to block this malicious activity, he says. And the volume is only increasing. Segura conducted research analyzing traffic hitting retailers' product pages and found that 91% were actually bad bots.

Taking legal action is difficult when it's nearly impossible to differentiate legitimate and illegitimate activity, which puts even more pressure on businesses. Scraping product pages or ticket scalping remains "kind of a gray area in terms of the legal aspect," Segura explains, adding that the law isn't quite clear yet on what is permitted.

In some cases, the culprits are organized groups just looking to make money and oftentimes use loopholes to circumvent the law. For example, they end up using existing infrastructure to collect scarce products and resell them, Segura says.

Threat actors organize so that they have specialties, just as defenders do, he has observed. Some specialize in reverse engineering specific parts of a website's code to understand how it works. Others focus on providing the necessary infrastructure, including all the IP addresses, to carry out those kinds of attacks, he says.

"You can source IPs from real users that are extremely convincing because they're also shared by humans," Segura explains. "So all these specializations within these groups, working well together, and making sure everybody's getting paid, is really interesting."

Behavioral analytics are struggling right now, London says, and is a "pain point" rippling across the industry.

Some bots can move the mouse pointer and send keystrokes to mimic typing, so verification techniques like measuring mouse movements or typing speeds need to evolve. Models can be a bit slow, just as humans can be, he notes.

"Although they are robotic in nature, some of those behavioral or human factors that teams have been using for indication points are really close," London says.

Since it's so difficult to determine whether activity is from a human or a bot, organizations should manage them both the same way when it comes to privileged identity: the less access, the better.

Given all of the risks and potential blast radii, "security teams, not developers, should probably decide whether AI is allowed in an organization," London recommends.

"From a security perspective, it makes it somewhat simple because AI agents can do bad things [and] humans can do bad things," he says. "So if we just look at it through that perspective, I don't care if it's a human or an agent."

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

#9696. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

Small English STT + LLM + TTS cascade with latency charts

TTS systems evaluated on objective metrics.

Congrats on the launch — running this cleanly on an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off is genuinely impressive. As a German speaker I'm happy to see it top the intelligibility ranking in German; the compounding is unforgiving to TTS, so that's not a small win.

One line in "what's next" I keep coming back to: Korean, Arabic and Japanese get offered as custom-training requests. That framing quietly shows where the field's centre of gravity still sits — a handful of languages are first-class citizens, and everything else is a sales conversation. The Open TTS Leaderboard covering 23 languages is a great step, but the long tail of the world's languages is still waiting. Would love to see lower-resource languages get first-class leaderboard slots rather than a custom quote.

#9695. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy Review: Pros and Cons

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

  • You get paid the same day you make a sale. Sellfy doesn't delay your funds as some other payment processors do. 
  • Print-on-demand services are available directly from your store, so you can sell merchandise to fans without setting up an integration. 
  • You can conduct all store-related activities via the mobile app and all online stores have mobile responsive designs.
  • Everything you need to make your website is included, including a custom domain name hosting, security for your files, and the ability to customize your store
  • The file security features can help you protect your digital property by allowing you to put PDF stamps, set download limits, and SSL encryption.

#9693. Attackers Target .NET Developers With Poisoned Job Assessments

Researchers discovered 13 malicious NuGet packages as part of a fake recruitment campaign that spreads malware and gives attackers access to developers' machines.

A coordinated supply chain campaign is targeting .NET developers with fake coding assignments, weaponized software dependencies, and GitHub-hosted malware capable of stealing browser credentials and establishing remote access.

Researchers at Socket discovered the campaign, which involves 13 malicious NuGet packages designed to compromise Windows-based developer environments through seemingly legitimate job assessments, according to a report published this week. The packages use fake job "Home Assessment" projects to target Windows .NET developers, with most posing as button controls for WinUI 3 and WPF, which are user interface frameworks for building applications.

"In the versions we analyzed, building or running a project that uses them downloads files from GitHub, stages a DLL side-loading pair around the Microsoft On-Screen Keyboard (osk.exe), or downloads and runs an executable," Socket researcher Kush Pandya wrote in the report.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

As in similar campaigns that weaponize developer repositories and code packages, attackers are exploiting developers' willingness to download, build, and run code they believe to be trustworthy. In this case, the malicious code is disguised as part of job-recruitment exercises for .NET developers. Such campaigns can turn routine development activities into infection vectors, potentially spreading malware and malicious code through the software supply chain.

NuGet is a package manager for .NET. Socket researchers traced the campaign across NuGet, GitHub repositories, and malicious code embedded in development projects, identifying packages linked through shared attack infrastructure and techniques.

The most recent example they found was a GitHub repository created on Nov. 4 that contained a purported WinUI 3 assessment called "Mini File Vault & Tracker." The project instructed candidates to complete a three- to four-hour development exercise using a supplied Visual Studio project. However, its dependencies contained malicious code.

"Candidates are told that building the project shows the starter UI and that the work must be developed and tested on native Windows with Visual Studio 2026," Pandya wrote in the report.

Socket could not determine how the Home Assessment lures reached candidates, as researchers found "no recruiter message, email or job post for them," he added.

The attack involved two malicious NuGet packages working together. One executed code after every project build, while the other launched a staged executable when the application created its button control. This effectively turned an ordinary development workflow into an infection chain.

Related:AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

The investigation eventually uncovered 13 unique package names and 28 versions across those packages, as well as four NuGet publisher accounts linked to the operation.

Characterizing the campaign as posing a very serious threat to enterprises, Pandya says attackers could gain access to a "treasure trove" of sensitive information by compromising a developer's machine.

"A developer's machine holds source code, SSH keys, GitHub, package registry and cloud tokens, and browser sessions that have often already passed multifactor authentication," Pandya tells Dark Reading. "In this campaign, building the take-home project was enough to run the threat actor's code."

Beyond access to terminals and configuration files, many developers who work from a console have their command history automatically collected, he says. This can give adversaries insight into the commands developers have executed, as well as access to passwords and API keys that may have been inadvertently pasted into the command line, he adds.

Related:Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Moreover, by disguising their activity as legitimate development work, attackers gain a degree of stealth and control once the malicious code is running on a developer's machine, he says.

"A threat actor could extract SSH keys and network configurations, but their access is still from an external host and must go through various security controls," Pandya explains. "If they are working directly from a developer's machine, they not only have the necessary access keys but also the expected IP address and geolocation to avoid suspicion."

As adversaries continue to weaponize code packages from legitimate sources to compromise the software supply chain, developers and security teams must remain vigilant. Socket has recommendations for both.

Developers should treat take-home coding assignments and unfamiliar projects as untrusted code, Pandya advises. Before building them, they should check for unfamiliar NuGet dependencies, additional package sources, and build scripts that could execute automatically.

"Open take-home tests and unfamiliar repositories only in a disposable virtual machine with no credentials," he recommends. "Restrict which package sources projects can use, scan dependencies before they are installed, and verify recruiters through official channels."

Organizations should also restrict which NuGet feeds developers can use and review third-party packages that contain build scripts capable of executing commands, according to Socket. They should also educate employees and job candidates about fake recruitment assessments to reduce the risk of attackers exploiting the hiring process to gain access to developer environments.

Security teams, meanwhile, should identify affected developer machines and treat suspected infections as potential credential and software supply chain compromises, rather than simply malware incidents, Pandya says.

"If a machine is compromised, isolate and reimage it, rotate credentials and tokens from a clean device, revoke active sessions, and review audit logs," he says.

#9692. Cyprus Becomes Espionage Target for Iranian Hackers

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

A previously undocumented Iranian threat group called "Volant Manticore" is targeting Cypriot organizations as part of an intelligence-gathering effort for Tehran.

Cyprus' growing security ties with Israel and its use as a staging ground for Western forces operating across the Middle East appear to be making the island an increasingly attractive target for Iranian cyber espionage.

Volant Manticore is an early example of that interest. The previously undocumented advanced persistent threat (APT) group has been targeting organizations in Cyprus as part of what researchers at Check Point describe as an Iranian intelligence-gathering campaign focused on the island.

Its targets so far have included a Cyprus-based airline operating primarily between Cyprus and Israel, telecommunications providers, critical infrastructure organizations, and a suspected government entity with military connections. The selection of targets suggests an effort to gather intelligence on the island's government, infrastructure, and relationships with regional partners, the researchers said.

Related:Latin America Sees Cyberattacks on Ports, Pipelines & Manufacturing

Check Point has assessed with medium confidence that Volant Manticore is likely an offshoot of the Iranian threat group MuddyWater, tasked primarily with spying on Cypriot organizations on behalf of Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS). It is among the first known Iranian groups to have a dedicated focus on Cyprus, although it has recently expanded its targeting to organizations in Saudi Arabia, says Sergey Shykevich, director of threat intelligence at Check Point Software.

"Cyprus' defense and energy ties with Israel and Greece, along with its role in Western military operations in the region, may help explain why it is a target for intelligence gathering," Shykevich says.

He points to a Check Point report from earlier this year on a surge in attempts by Iran-linked actors to exploit vulnerabilities in Internet-connected surveillance cameras across the Middle East, including Cyprus, beginning on Feb. 28, when US and Israeli strikes against Iran began. Access to the cameras could have provided Iranian intelligence with a way to monitor military and other strategically important facilities, gather information ahead of potential attacks, and assess the damage from strikes afterward. "The timing is another indication of how Iranian cyber activity tracks with security developments in the region," Shykevich adds.

Check Point described Volant Manticore as relying heavily on phishing to gain an initial foothold using lures tailored for the organizations and sectors it targets. The security vendor's investigation of the group began when it spotted a fabricated resume on VirusTotal associated with "Athena Marinou," a fictitious, AI-generated travel-and-tourism professional.

Related:Nok et norsk energiselskap har blitt utsatt for et datainnbrudd på to dager

The document directed recipients to download the full CV from what appeared to be a legitimate recruitment website. The link, however, pointed to an archive hosted on Catbox, which delivered KuboShell — a custom backdoor that the group is using to establish an initial foothold on compromised systems, conduct basic reconnaissance, and receive commands from its operators.

Check Point found that the Windows-based backdoor uses the decentralized InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for command-and-control (C2) communications, potentially making them harder to block or disrupt than communications routed through a conventional attacker-controlled server. The malware allows attackers to collect details about compromised systems and networks using basic PowerShell instructions. Check Point found evidence that the group then deployed a more extensive, multistage post-compromise toolkit it calls the Homa Framework.

Volant Manticore also uses legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) software such as N-able, NetLock, and MeshCentral in its campaigns. The tools enable remote access and administrative capabilities while allowing the attacks to blend in with legitimate traffic. Check Point also identified infrastructure associated with credential-harvesting campaigns, including domains designed to resemble corporate email services. The researchers found evidence of operators testing their malware against antivirus products and using virtual machines and VPN-related software in their operational environments.

Related:Second Norwegian Energy Company Breached in 2 Days

Check Point's analysis showed overlaps between Volant Manticore's techniques and code and those used by the long-active Iranian group MuddyWater. However, Check Point assessed Volant Manticore is a separate operation likely run by former MuddyWater members. "The group has a well-developed toolkit that combines techniques we’ve seen from MuddyWater with tools it developed itself," Shykevich says. "One of the less common techniques we observed was its use of KuboShell, a backdoor that provides remote access and communicates through IPFS, a decentralized file-sharing network."

In September, Check Point observed the group suddenly broadening its focus to include Saudi Arabia. "We are currently seeing the group active in both countries," Shykevich says. While Cyprus remains its primary espionage target, the group has been targeting Saudi organizations as well, mainly in the healthcare sector, he adds. "The increase in activity coincided with escalating tensions between Saudi Arabia and the Iranian-backed Houthis. The scale of the group's activity in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere is likely to vary as the situation in the region evolves."

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

#9691. AntSeed Review 2027: Cheapest Way to Run an OpenClaw & Hermes Agent 24/7 on Pay-Per-Request Model

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AI, Web3, Cybersecurity, Startup Funding & Enterprise SaaS. Top Journalist, Analyst & Thought Leadership Media Leader.

AntSeed is a peer-to-peer market for AI inference that lets an always-on agent like OpenClaw or Hermes send every model call to the cheapest verified provider on the network. Instead of one company setting the price, independent providers list the same open models at their own prices, and a local proxy sends each request to the cheapest provider that meets the buyer's minimum trust score. AntSeed's own calculation for a coding agent's month of usage puts Claude Opus 5.5 at 93% below list price on its network and Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 89% below, based on advertised prices in mid-November 2026. For an agent that makes hundreds of calls a day, that difference compounds, which is why the model layer decides the cheapest way to run an AI agent 24/7.

Verdict: AntSeed is built for OpenClaw and Hermes users who run open models around the clock and want the model bill to fall through price competition. It asks for a little more setup than a hosted API, and it rewards that setup on every call.

AntSeed is a peer-to-peer network for AI services. Providers announce their models and prices on a distributed hash table, the same kind of discovery system BitTorrent uses. Buyers run a local endpoint that finds those providers and sends requests to them over encrypted peer-to-peer connections. There is no central aggregator between buyer and provider.

AntSeed says the network offers more than 700 models, and its live count in mid-November 2026 was 703 models from 95 providers, including image and video models. The Antseed Foundation has raised $2.4M in a token round led by Spark Capital, with participation from Collider, DCG, North Island Ventures, Reciprocal Ventures, Relayer Capital, and Venice.ai.

The network is in real use. According to AntSeed's on-chain figures, it averaged about 31.7 billion tokens and 434,000 requests a day from 9 to 15 November 2026. In the 30 days to 15 November, 692 paying wallets paid about $76,800 to 104 different providers over that period. AntSeed notes that paid token counts are a lower bound, because they only include usage that buyers report on-chain.

Routing is the reason AntSeed suits a 24/7 agent. According to AntSeed's documentation, the local proxy sends each request to the cheapest provider that meets the buyer's minimum trust score (60 out of 100 by default), unless the buyer pins a specific provider. Providers that are cooling down or have recently failed are moved down the list, so another provider takes the request.

For an always-on agent, this changes the cost model. A single-provider API charges one price for every call. On AntSeed, every call is a fresh choice among competing providers, so the agent pays the lowest price available at that moment for the model it asked for.

The local endpoint speaks both the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs, so an agent connects to it the way it would connect to any compatible provider. The setup has four steps, followed by AntSeed's recommended gateway option.

Install the AntSeed command-line tool on the agent's machine with npm install -g @antseed/cli, which needs Node.js 20 or later. AntSeed also publishes an agent-readable setup skill, so an agent can follow the installation steps itself. On a personal computer, the AntSeed desktop app runs the same local endpoint.

Running antseed buyer start launches the local buyer proxy at http://127.0.0.1:8377/v1, which works only on the same machine as the agent. If your agent runs on a VPS, install AntSeed on the same server so the agent can reach the endpoint on localhost.

For any OpenAI-compatible agent, set the base URL to the local endpoint and use the placeholder API key antseed-p2p, since the local endpoint does not validate one.

For OpenClaw, AntSeed's integration guide adds the antseed provider to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json, after which a model can be selected with a command such as openclaw models set "antseed/kimi-k2.6", followed by openclaw gateway restart.

For Hermes, AntSeed is registered as a custom provider in ~/.hermes/config.yaml following AntSeed's Hermes integration guide, then Hermes is restarted to load it.

Providers are always paid per request in USDC on Base. The command-line proxy is funded with USDC only, and antseed buyer deposit shows the funding address. The gateway and the desktop app also take card top-ups of $1 to $200 where available, and no AntSeed account is needed for either.

AntSeed now recommends the gateway for agents. Run antseed gateway service install, then antseed gateway key create --label openclaw, and point the agent at http://localhost:8379/v1. Each agent gets its own key and budget. For OpenClaw without funds, the model antseed/@preset/openclaw tries free providers first. Some providers offer free models.

AntSeed has no subscription. The agent pays per request, at the price of the provider that serves it. The total depends on which models the agent uses and how many calls it makes.

Live prices are listed on AntSeedStats, an independent tracker that lists network prices for each model next to its official API price. AntSeed's own calculation for a coding agent's month of 22 million input and 5.5 million output tokens shows the gap:

Across 192 models with a published list price, AntSeedStats showed a median saving of 52% on 12 November 2026. AntSeed's figures use advertised prices and the cheapest provider that passes its default trust minimum, so they are not measured per request. Prices move as providers join and compete, so check the live rates before estimating a budget.

For a 24/7 agent, the per-call saving matters most on background traffic. OpenClaw's default heartbeat runs every 30 minutes, which is 48 model calls a day before the agent does any real work. Each of those calls goes to the cheapest qualifying provider.

It turns price into competition. The same open model can be served by several providers, and the agent pays the lowest qualifying price on each request rather than a fixed list price.

It keeps the agent unchanged. OpenClaw and Hermes keep their configuration, memory and tools. Only the model endpoint changes, and switching back is a matter of pointing the agent at a different base URL.

It adds resilience. Because many providers serve the same model, a provider that fails does not stop the agent. The proxy moves on to another one.

It scales with the network. As more providers join, the price competition for popular models increases.

AntSeed runs locally. The endpoint has to run next to the agent, which is one more process to keep alive on the server. A hosted aggregator such as OpenRouter needs nothing running on your machine.

Prices vary by provider and over time. That is the point of the market, but it means the cost of a given model is a live figure, not a fixed list price.

The model range depends on providers. Popular open models are well covered, while a niche model may have few sellers or none.

The same network also serves teams building AI apps. AntSeed's gateway for apps sits in front of an existing OpenAI- or Anthropic-based app through the Chat Completions, Responses and Messages APIs, so switching means changing the API address, key and model rather than rewriting code. It can run on a developer's computer or on a server.

What the gateway adds is control. Each app gets its own key, and spending limits can be set per key, per team member or per workspace, by day, week, month or lifetime. Keys can allow only certain models, allow or block certain providers, and cap the price per million input, output and cached input tokens, as well as the price per image. Provider ranking and fallback rules are configurable too. With automatic routing, a request that fails with a retryable error can move to another provider before streaming starts. Balances can be topped up by card or USDC, with no AntSeed account needed. For a 24/7 agent that has become part of a product, such as a support agent, this is the layer that shows what each app costs and stops one runaway app from draining the budget for the rest.

AntSeed is the strongest choice for builders running OpenClaw, Hermes or another OpenAI-compatible agent around the clock on open models, who want the lowest per-request price and are comfortable running one local endpoint. Teams shipping AI apps can put the same network behind each app through the gateway, with a key and a budget for every app.

It is less suited to someone who wants a single hosted API key with nothing to install, or who needs a model that few providers serve.

Host the agent on a low-cost or free server and keep the model bill down, since it is usually the bigger cost. Running open models through AntSeed sends each call to the cheapest verified provider on the network. Routing heartbeats to a small or free model and lengthening the heartbeat interval cuts background spend further.

Yes. OpenClaw and Hermes both have maintained AntSeed setup skills and integration guides. Any other agent that speaks the OpenAI or Anthropic API can connect by pointing its custom provider settings at the local endpoint.

OpenRouter passes through each provider's list price, charging a fee when you buy credits. On AntSeed, independent providers compete on price for every request. The independent tracker AntSeedStats showed a median saving of 52% against list prices across 192 models on 12 November 2026. The saving for your agent depends on the models it uses.

Yes. Install AntSeed on the same server as the agent and start the local endpoint there, so the agent reaches it on localhost. This is the simplest setup for a 24/7 agent.

Providers are paid per request in USDC on Base. The command-line proxy takes USDC only, while the gateway and the desktop app also accept card top-ups of $1 to $200, handled by Crossmint and not available in every region. No AntSeed account is needed. Some providers offer free models. There is no subscription.

Yes. AntSeed's gateway for apps works with existing OpenAI- and Anthropic-based apps by changing the API address, key and model. Each app gets its own key and spending limit, and requests are routed across the same competing providers that serve agents.
